frame: Commander Rhee's log from the space station has been beamed to the Soggy Biscuit's radio.
text: Station log, day forty-one. This morning we passed over the middle of Australia just as the sun came up, and I floated by the window for the whole twelve minutes it took to cross. From four hundred kilometres up, the desert looked enormous and completely empty, a rusty brown that stretched from one edge of the window to the other. Then I spotted the river. It is one of the longest rivers on the continent, thousands of kilometres from end to end, yet from up here it wound across the desert like a loose thread dropped on a brown carpet. It was a thin, dark green line, curling back on itself again and again, and in places it almost disappeared. I tried to photograph it, but the camera kept focusing on a smudge where my nose had touched the glass. My crewmate Jo says I spend more time at the window than at my experiments. She is probably right. Tomorrow we pass over the reef, and I have already cleaned the glass. Jo has asked me to stop pressing my face against it, but I can't promise anything. The reef is meant to be the best view of the whole mission, and I don't intend to miss a second of it.

frame: This sign stands at the start of the Mirage Mangroves boardwalk. The Metapince lives under it.
text: WELCOME TO THE MIRAGE MANGROVES BOARDWALK. Please stay on the boardwalk and keep dogs on a lead. Look down between the planks and you will see a tangle of roots poking out of the mud, some thin and some thick. It may look like a muddy, smelly swamp, but this forest is the nursery of the sea. When the tide comes in, thousands of baby fish, prawns and crabs swim in among the roots. The roots are too tight and twisted for big hungry fish to follow, so the babies can feed and grow in safety. Some will spend months here. When they are big enough, they swim out through the channel to the open water and the reef beyond, and many of the fish caught off the end of the jetty started their lives right under your feet. Nobody plants these trees or sells them; they have grown here on their own for hundreds of years. Scientists have counted more than fifty kinds of fish living in this one small forest. Please do not pull up seedlings, dig for crabs or throw rubbish into the water. Without these trees, there would be far fewer fish in the sea, so please help us protect them. Thank you for visiting.

text: After four months at the rescue centre, Crumpet the green turtle was finally ready to go home. She had come to us in winter, tangled in fishing line and far too thin, and it had taken weeks of care and a great many squid before she was strong enough to swim properly again. On release day, six of us carried her down to the beach in a padded crate, while a small crowd gathered on the sand. The morning was calm and bright. As we set the crate down at the edge of the water, the sea opened its arms to her. Gentle waves rolled up the sand, curled around her flippers and coaxed her forward, as if the whole sea had been waiting for her to come home. Crumpet paused for a moment and lifted her head. Then she pushed off into the shallows, and the water folded itself softly around her shell. A few seconds later, she surfaced once, took a breath and was gone. Nobody on the beach said anything for a while. Then the youngest volunteer, who had fed Crumpet every morning, burst into happy tears. We will miss her, but she is exactly where she belongs.

frame: Poet Pip wrote a poem after her dive on the reef. The Plonkett can't swim that deep, so it stayed in the boat.
text:
REEF DIVE
by Poet Pip

We roll backwards off the boat,
into a world of green and blue.
The chain clanks against the hull.
Then everything goes quiet.
Pale coral, chalky white and cinnamon brown,
stretches out beneath us.

Bright blue butterflyfish bob below.
Kelp curls and coils in the current.
We float above the coral bed.
A turtle bumps me on the head.

An octopus peers out of a crack,
then squeezes in and won't come back.
Our air runs low, it's time to rise.
We climb aboard with salty eyes.

Poet Pip says she wrote the poem on the boat ride home, with a wet towel round her shoulders, and she read it out loud to herself again and again. 'A poem isn't finished,' she says, 'until it sounds right in your mouth.' She changed one line six times before she was happy with it.

frame: Indi found this story pinned to the bakery noticeboard on Harbour Lane. The Moodgill's fins went from grey to gold.
text: Rain had been falling on Harbour Lane since breakfast, and by four o'clock the whole street looked like a photo left out in the sun to fade. Umbrellas hurried past with their heads down. Shop windows fogged over. A busker stood under the bakery awning with a battered violin case open at his feet, holding three coins and a bus ticket. Nobody looked at him. A delivery van splashed through a puddle and soaked his shoes. For a while he just tuned his strings, as if he wasn't sure anyone wanted to hear. Then he began to play. The music spilled out like warm light from an open door. A woman with a pram slowed down. A man in a soggy suit stopped checking his phone. A little boy in a yellow raincoat let go of his dad's hand and started stomping in a puddle, perfectly in time, sending up splashes that glittered under the streetlights. The baker came out, wiping her hands on her apron, and leaned in the doorway to listen. When the song ended, people clapped with wet hands and dropped coins into the case until it rattled. The rain hadn't stopped. Somehow, nobody seemed to mind anymore. The busker played until the streetlights came on.
